title: The POKEY registers, write and read
covers: the registers of the Atari C012294 POKEY as the Atari 400/800 Hardware Manual describes them, and MAME's handling of each

rows.text: AUDF1, AUDF2, AUDF3 and AUDF4 are the audio frequency registers at D200, D202, D204 and D206.
A write puts data into the four frequency control registers, each of which controls a divide-by-N counter.
N is one greater than the binary number in the frequency register.
All bits zero give N = 1 and all bits one give N = 256.
AUDC1, AUDC2, AUDC3 and AUDC4 are the audio channel control registers at D201, D203, D205 and D207.
A write puts data into the four control registers, each controlling the noise content and volume of its channel.
The table pairs hex 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, A and C with a distortion source and a divisor N set by the frequency register.
A value with bit 4 set forces the output on: volume only.
The low four bits select one of sixteen volume levels: 0 is the lowest (off), 8 half and F the highest.
MAME enters the audio writes through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
A write to an AUDC register also marks the raw output for recalculation.
POT0 to POT7 are the pot value registers at D200 to D207.
They read the value of 8 pots (paddle controllers) connected to the 8-line pot port, from 0 to 228.
The paddles are numbered from left to right, and turning a knob clockwise decreases its value.
The values are valid only after 228 TV lines following POTGO, or after ALLPOT changes.
The OS keeps shadows in PADDL0 to PADDL7 at hex 270 to 277.
A read of one of these addresses returns that pot's value.
MAME enters the pot reads through a switch on the low four bits and takes the pot number from the low three.
MAME returns the measured value once the pot's ALLPOT bit is set, and the pot counter value before then.
AUDCTL is the Audio Mode Control Register at D208.
A write to D208 puts data into the Audio Mode Control Register.
D7, stored, changes the 17-bit polynomial into a 9-bit one.
D6, stored, clocks channel 1 with 1.79 MHz instead of 64 kHz.
D5, stored, clocks channel 3 with 1.79 MHz instead of 64 kHz.
D4, stored, clocks channel 2 with channel 1 instead of 64 kHz, a 16-bit counter.
D3, stored, clocks channel 4 with channel 3 instead of 64 kHz, a 16-bit counter.
D2, stored, inserts a high-pass filter in channel 1, clocked by channel 3.
D1, stored, inserts a high-pass filter in channel 2, clocked by channel 4.
D0, stored, changes the normal 64 kHz frequency into 15 kHz.
The exact clock frequencies are 1.78979 MHz, 63.9210 kHz and 15.6999 kHz (NTSC; PAL differs).
The output frequency is Fin/2N, where N is the value in the frequency register plus one.
With 1.79 MHz a modified formula Fin/(2(AUDF+M)) takes M as 4 for an 8-bit counter and 7 for a 16-bit one.
MAME enters AUDCTL through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
A write of the value already stored returns before storing it.
A write stores the byte in m_AUDCTL, marks the raw output for recalculation and logs the value.
ALLPOT at D208 reads the present state of the 8-line pot port.
The capacitor dump transistors must be turned off by going to fast pot scan mode (bit 2 of SKCTL) or by starting pot scan (POTGO).
Each bit is one pot's flag: 0 means the pot register value is valid, 1 that it is not.
A read of D208 returns the eight pot line states.
MAME enters the ALLPOT read through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
While the two low bits of SKCTL are zero, MAME returns m_ALLPOT; with a board callback it stores and returns its value; otherwise it returns the register inverted.
STIMER is the start timer register at D209.
A write to D209 resets all audio frequency dividers to their AUDF value.
The dividers generate timer interrupts when they count down to zero, if IRQEN enables them.
MAME enters STIMER through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
MAME zeroes each channel output and sets its filter sample to 1 on channels 1 and 2, 0 on 3 and 4.
KBCODE at D209 reads the keyboard code.
It is usually read in response to a keyboard interrupt, bit 6 or bit 7 of IRQST.
Bit 7 is the control key and bit 6 the shift key.
A read of D209 returns the keyboard code; the OS reads it into shadow CH and a get-character function converts it to ATASCII.
MAME enters the keyboard code read through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
SKRES is the serial port reset register at D20A, with no data bits.
A write to D20A resets bits 7, 6 and 5 of the serial port and keyboard status register to 1.
MAME enters SKRES through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
MAME keeps the status active high internally and clears there what the status reads as bits 7, 6 and 5.
RANDOM is the random number generator register at D20A.
A read returns the high-order 8 bits of a 17-bit polynomial counter, or of a 9-bit one if bit 7 of AUDCTL is set.
MAME enters the random read through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
POTGO is the start pot scan register at D20B; no data bits are used.
A write to D20B starts the pot scan sequence, the scan counter cleared to zero.
The document asks that the pot values be read before the write.
The capacitor dump transistors turn off at the start of the scan and on again when the counter reaches 228.
The scan counter counts, and each pot's value is captured in its register when its line crosses the trigger voltage.
The OS vertical blank code writes this register.
MAME starts the scan only when the two low bits of SKCTL are not both zero, and then clears ALLPOT and the scan counter at once.
Nothing in MAME models the capacitor dump transistors the document turns off at the start and on again at 228.
MAME counts to 228 and marks a pot as the counter passes its value, but a read before the mark returns the running counter, not a captured value.
MAME takes each pot's value from the board's callback, capped at 228, or 228 when there is none.
MAME enters the scan from the POTGO case; the routine logs, loops over the eight pots and marks a pot ready when its callback returns 0.
SEROUT is the 8-bit parallel holding register for serial output data at D20D.
A write to D20D puts a byte into the holding register, transferred to the output shift register once the previous byte is transmitted.
A write is usually made in response to the serial output data interrupt, bit 4 of IRQST.
MAME enters SEROUT through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
When the two low bits of SKCTL are not both zero, MAME marks the output register full.
SERIN at D20D reads the 8-bit parallel holding register loaded by a received byte.
A read is usually made in response to the serial input interrupt, bit 5 of IRQST.
A read of D20D returns the received byte.
MAME enters the serial input read through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
IRQEN is the interrupt enable register at D20E.
A write to D20E puts data into the interrupt enable bits: 0 disables an interrupt and sets its IRQST bit to 1, 1 enables it.
D7 enables the break key interrupt, D6 the other key, D5 serial input data ready and D4 serial output data needed.
D3 enables the transmission-finished interrupt, D2 timer 4, D1 timer 2 and D0 timer 1.
The OS keeps a copy in POKMSK at hex 10.
The document advises changing one bit of POKMSK with AND or OR and storing the value in both IRQEN and POKMSK.
MAME enters IRQEN through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
MAME asserts the interrupt line when the transmission-finished bit is enabled and set, and clears it when no enabled bit is set.
MAME stores the mask and clears the set status bits it disables, but the transmission-finished bit stays pending, reading 0 where the document sets it to 1.
IRQST at D20E reads the interrupt status register.
A read gives the status bits: 0 means an interrupt, 1 no interrupt.
D7 is the break key, D6 the other key, D5 serial input ready and D4 serial output needed.
D3 is transmission finished, D2 timer 4, D1 timer 2 and D0 timer 1.
Bit 3 generates two stop bits and has no direct reset.
MAME enters the status read through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
MAME keeps the status active high internally and returns it inverted.
SKCTL at D20F controls the configuration of the serial port, the fast pot scan and the keyboard enable.
A write to D20F puts data into the register that controls the serial port, the fast pot scan and the keyboard enable.
The bits are normally zero and perform their functions when true.
D7 is force break: the serial output is forced to zero (space).
D6, D5 and D4 are the serial port mode control, described by the mode chart on page II.34.
D3 is two tone: the serial output is transmitted as a two tone signal instead of logic true and false.
D2 is fast pot scan: the scan completes in two TV line times instead of one frame time, and the dump transistors are disabled.
D1 enables keyboard scanning.
D0 enables keyboard debounce.
D0 and D1 both zero initialize the chip, the state used for testing and initializing it.
The OS keeps a shadow at SSKCTL, hex 232.
The document advises writing hex 13 to both SKCTL and SSKCTL after I/O, since an aborted cassette operation may leave the two tone bit set.
Note: powered on, the serial output may stay low even with the break bit cleared; sending a byte (00 or FF recommended) makes it high.
Note: POKEY has no reset pin and no original power-on state.
MAME enters SKCTL through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
A write of the value already stored returns before storing it.
With the two low bits zero, MAME clears IRQEN and the status bits, the polynomial and clock counters, sets the serial shifters to 1 and clears the busy bit.
When keyboard scanning is off, MAME clears the keyboard-pressed bit and the keyboard counters.
MAME sets the input clock line true when the input clock bits are zero, and the output clock line false when the output clock bits are zero.
In asynchronous mode with the serial input not busy, MAME resets channels 3 and 4.
When the serial input is not busy and two tone is off, MAME drives the serial data line low for a break and high otherwise.
MAME marks the raw output for recalculation.
SKSTAT at D20F reads the status register of the serial port and keyboard.
The bits are normally true and give these facts when zero.
D7 is a serial data input frame error, D6 a serial input over-run and D5 a keyboard over-run, reset by SKRES.
D4 is the serial input line, D3 the shift key, D2 the last key still depressed and D1 the serial shift register busy.
D0 is not used and reads as logic true.
MAME enters the serial status read through a switch on the low four bits of the offset.
MAME keeps the status active high internally and returns it inverted.
